teaser.text: Thermo Fisher Scientific sells the means of doing biology, medicine and laboratory testing. Its business becomes clearer when you follow a customer’s dollar from a repeated supply purchase or a large instrument to the services, staff and materials that deliver it.

stock.opening: The weighted forecast is $633.20 in October 2027, $658.58 in October 2028, and $681.35 in October 2029, with the base case at 53% probability. It hinges on broader organic recovery, profitable acquisition integration, and enough cash generation to support investment and shareholder returns.
stock.closing: The full memo also explains Thermo Fisher Scientific’s business, rivals, management, and risks.

blocks.heading: Where could Thermo Fisher Scientific’s shares be by 2029?

paragraphs.text: The bear case has 27% probability. The base case has 53%; the bull case has 20%. On October 21, 2026, third-quarter results test whether organic growth is tracking management’s expected second-half pace of roughly 4% and whether cash generation is improving. Decisive evidence includes repeat bioproduction orders—making medicines or their ingredients with living cells—PPD awards converting into paid work, and Clario customers adopting combined services. Clario’s $125 million fixed payment is due in January 2027. By its fifth anniversary, the test is whether expected synergies—savings or added earnings expected when combined businesses work together—have produced $175 million of annual adjusted operating income.

The weighted value is $633.20 in October 2027, a 4% loss including dividends. It reaches $658.58 in October 2028, broadly flat including dividends. By October 2029, the weighted value is $681.35, a 4% gain.

blocks.heading: What has to go right for Thermo Fisher Scientific?

paragraphs.text: Base revenue starts at $47,750 million in 2026. It grows 5% annually. Margins rise from 14.5% in 2027 to 14.9% in 2029. Base earnings therefore reach $7,270 million in 2027 and $8,237 million in 2029; the middle year is $7,740 million. The bear case uses low-single-digit growth and margins around 13.4%–13.5%, producing $6,575 million in 2027 and $6,880 million in 2029. The bull case uses 7% annual growth and margins rising from 15.0% to 16.0%, producing $7,664 million and $9,360 million. Q2 organic growth reached 5% across all four segments, supporting the base, but earlier organic growth was negative in 2023 and flat in 2024.

The bull case requires several successes at once. Research and manufacturing demand broadens, repeat bioproduction orders return, PPD and Clario convert work profitably, and cross-selling improves margins and cash flow. The bull value is $756.25 in 2027. It reaches $921.02 in 2029, including dividends. Its probability is 20% because sustained 7% growth, margin expansion, deleveraging and acquisition returns all remain uncertain.

paragraphs.text: Thermo Fisher remains a strong cash generator, but its earnings recovery did not produce stronger free cash flow in 2025.

blocks.heading: How much does Thermo Fisher Scientific pay per share?

paragraphs.text: The dividend begins at $1.72 per share. Base growth of 10% produces $1.89 in 2027 and $2.29 in 2029. The bear pauses at $1.72 before reaching $1.77, while the bull uses 12% growth to reach $2.42. Five straight annual increases and a low historical cash burden support continued growth, although debt and investment needs justify a slower base assumption.

blocks.heading: Is Thermo Fisher Scientific's dividend covered by its cash?

paragraphs.text: The pattern is important because shareholder payments and acquisitions competed for the same cash. A buyback removes shares, so future earnings are divided among fewer owners; that can lift earnings per share, but creates value only when the company buys at a sensible price. Money used for buybacks cannot simultaneously fund a factory, an acquisition or debt reduction.

blocks.heading: What could change Thermo Fisher Scientific's dividend?

paragraphs.text: The base case becomes more credible if organic growth remains within the 3%–6% near-term range and repeat orders gradually lift segment revenue. It would also require cash generation to fund investment and shareholder returns while debt stabilizes.

blocks.heading: What is Thermo Fisher Scientific's dividend yield today?

paragraphs.text: Revenue shows the pandemic surge and recovery. Operating margin improved, but the latest margin remains below its earlier peak. Real free cash flow, computed from the company’s cash-flow statement as cash from operations minus capital spending, declined in 2025 as the latest acquisition period increased net debt. The price is $662.09. Trailing P/E is 35.6x and forward P/E is 24.1x. Free-cash-flow yield is 2.6%; real free-cash-flow yield is 2.4%. Dividend yield is 0.3%; buyback yield is 1.2%.

blocks.heading: What has Thermo Fisher Scientific guided for 2026?

paragraphs.text: Thermo Fisher expects a GAAP effective tax rate of 9.0%–11.0% for 2026 and an adjusted rate of 11.5%. It also expects to pay $1,500 million in cash taxes, because some acquisition-related amortization lowers accounting profit without reducing taxable income.

Operating cash flow was $3,317 million in the first half of 2026, and free cash flow was $2,503 million. Free cash flow is operating cash left after net capital spending, so it is the cash engine for acquisitions, dividends, buybacks and debt reduction. Management’s full-year target is $6.9 billion–$7.4 billion. That requires approximately $4.4 billion–$4.9 billion in the second half.

blocks.heading: Has Thermo Fisher Scientific kept its past promises?

paragraphs.text: Some promises have bound. After Thermo Fisher reduced its external outlook during 2025, the compensation committee kept the original targets. The annual incentive and performance-stock programs therefore paid below target. The preceding completed performance-stock cycle paid zero for Casper and most other named executives.

blocks.heading: What have Thermo Fisher Scientific's last eight quarters shown?

paragraphs.text: The sequence of recent quarters strengthens the case for recovery. Reported year-on-year growth accelerated through June, and all four segments contributed. Comparing equivalent quarters is more useful than treating a single sequential change as a trend.

Cash supplied the more convincing confirmation. Operating cash rose to $2,125 million, even as capital spending increased to $450 million. Free cash flow reached $1,675 million. March also improved, though its EPS included a $175 million domestication tax benefit.
